episode_title: An 86-minute guide to finding PMF | Rob Snyder (Author, The Power of Pull)
description_html:
Rob Snyder is the author of The Power of Pull and writes the newsletter The Physics of Startups. He has advised more than 50 startups on growing from zero to $1 million in ARR, drawing on his own experience as a founder who spent two years pushing a product the market didn’t want before accidentally stumbling onto what actually works. In this episode, we walk step by step through his framework for finding product-market fit, from coming up with an idea to closing your first handful of deals.

We discuss:

1. The PULL framework: Project, Unavoidable, List of options, Limitations

2. Where the best startup ideas come from

3. Tactics for cold outreach and running your first sales call

4. Why Rob advises against design partners

5. Goblin mode: what to do when nothing is working

6. How to apply the PULL framework inside larger companies

—

summary.overview: Rob Snyder, author of The Power of Pull, presents a practical framework for finding product-market fit by identifying people who are already stuck on an urgent project and whose existing options are insufficient. He walks through idea generation, customer outreach, sales calls, pricing, retention, and scaling, arguing that founders should sell to learn whether customers pull the product from them rather than trying to persuade an indifferent market.

takeaways.heading: What pull means
takeaways.detail: Pull is not something a company possesses; it is something a specific person has. A customer has pull when they are trying to complete an urgent project, cannot do it with their existing tools or methods, and would find it strange not to buy a solution that unblocks them.

takeaways.heading: The PULL framework
takeaways.detail: P stands for project: the job on the person’s to-do list. U stands for unavoidable: why it must happen now. The first L is the list of options they considered, and the second L is why those options are insufficient.

takeaways.heading: All four are required
takeaways.detail: A project without urgency produces complaints but not purchases. An urgent project with adequate existing options also produces no sale; the person must be genuinely blocked by the alternatives available to them.

takeaways.heading: Find ideas firsthand
takeaways.detail: Snyder recommends getting close to the people and work involved rather than brainstorming abstract product ideas. One founder shadowed multiple industries, eventually spending days with physical therapists and even considering buying a franchise, before discovering a problem worth pursuing.

takeaways.heading: Write a hypothesis
takeaways.detail: Founders should state who is trying to do what, why it is unavoidable now, which options they considered, and why those options fail. They can then test the hypothesis with the person who inspired it and see whether that person actually tries to buy.

takeaways.heading: Test before building
takeaways.detail: Snyder strongly advises against building first, since founders need to face the cold wind of reality as soon as possible. He is skeptical of design partnerships because participants often give feedback without having an urgent project or ever becoming paying customers.

takeaways.heading: Use the Hail Mary
takeaways.detail: When a conversation is lukewarm, ask: “Is there anything on your to-do list that you would pay me to do right now?” This can reveal a different problem with real pull and has led some startups to pivot into their first contracts.

takeaways.heading: Cold outreach
takeaways.detail: Initial outreach should aim only to start an interesting conversation, not to sell the product. Snyder suggests a short, unusual message—such as mentioning a notable investor, background, or personal connection—and gives a rough benchmark of 30–40% connection acceptance and 30–50% replies among those who accept.

takeaways.heading: Sales-call structure
takeaways.detail: Start by asking why the person took the call, then agree on an agenda before asking discovery questions. The goal is to surface the person’s pull, not interrogate or convince them; a successful conversation ends with them asking how to move forward.

takeaways.heading: Recognize real interest
takeaways.detail: Leaned-in urgency matters more than enthusiasm or future-oriented politeness. “We could use this in Q4,” requests for more information, and general praise are not the same as “How do we get started?”

takeaways.heading: Close and price
takeaways.detail: After confirming fit, return with a rough concept and plan, which may initially be service-shaped rather than a finished platform. Pricing can be bounded by the value of completing the project or the cost of current alternatives; early on, Snyder prioritizes willingness to transact over optimizing price.

takeaways.heading: Goblin mode
takeaways.detail: If repeated calls reveal no pull, founders should analyze what they learned, ask Hail Mary questions, and form a new hypothesis. In emergencies, Snyder recommends “goblin mode”: unusually intense efforts such as traveling to conferences, visiting offices, or doing many meetings to find a real problem.

takeaways.heading: Retention after purchase
takeaways.detail: Customers are effectively guaranteed to churn until they reach a specific moment when it would be strange for them to leave. Founders should deliver the product firsthand, identify that retention milestone, and design onboarding so every customer reaches it.

takeaways.heading: The case-study factory
takeaways.detail: Snyder’s mental model for a startup is a factory that repeats one successful case study: finding the right prospects, converting them, delivering the promised outcome, and making them unlikely to churn. The current bottleneck—pipeline, close rate, or delivery—should determine the team’s focus.

takeaways.heading: Existing companies
takeaways.detail: The framework also applies to mature companies launching features or new products. Snyder recommends that founders or zero-to-one product leaders sell the proposed capability to existing customers before building it, using customer requests from sales conversations rather than relying on internal whiteboarding.

takeaways.heading: Tarpit ideas
takeaways.detail: Snyder warns against copying a category with a clear winner without a specific theory about being different. A product being somewhat better is insufficient if the target customer is not blocked or urgently seeking a change.
